title: The unskilled driver
theme: For one without understanding, whose mind is never held, the senses are out of control, like a poor driver’s vicious horses.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «यस्तु बुद्ध्याख्यः सारथिः», the charioteer called intellect

sandhi.rule: Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); u and i before a dissimilar vowel become v and y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि); n of -vān stays before bh.
a + i → e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); i before a dissimilar vowel → y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
āḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus remains.

morphology.note: vijñāna with the possessive suffix -vat (nom. sg. -vān), negated: ‘one who has no discernment’.
Genitive singular of the i-stem sārathi: -eḥ.

translation.literal: ‘But he who is without understanding, with a mind always unheld — his senses are uncontrollable, like the bad horses of a charioteer.’
translation.readable: ‘When the driver lacks understanding and never holds the mind steady, the senses run out of control, like a poor driver’s unbroken horses.’

anvaya: यः तु अविज्ञानवान् सदा अयुक्तेन मनसा भवति, तस्य इन्द्रियाणि सारथेः दुष्टाश्वाः इव अवश्यानि [भवन्ति] ॥
syntax: A relative clause (yas tu … bhavati) with its correlative tasya; the main clause has no verb, indriyāṇy avaśyāni being a nominal sentence, with the simile duṣṭāśvā iva sāratheḥ.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara on 1.3.5–6: the charioteer called intellect, «बुद्ध्याख्यः सारथिः». On 1.3.7–8 he takes the same words of the rider who has such a charioteer. Raṅgarāmānuja, commenting on 1.3.5–6 together, speaks of understanding and mind, as charioteer and reins, being sound or not: «सारथिप्रग्रहत्वेन रूपितयोः विज्ञान-मनसोः सामीचीन्ये».

beginner: Now the chariot picture is put to work. Imagine a driver who does not really know how to drive and who lets the reins hang loose all the time. The horses do whatever they like: they bolt, swerve and follow every distraction. That, says the verse, is what happens when a person's intellect lacks understanding and the mind is never steadied: the senses run wherever they are pulled. Śaṅkara takes 'the one without understanding' to be the intellect itself, the driver, and the loose mind to be slack reins. Raṅgarāmānuja comments on this verse and the next together: when the driver and the reins are sound, the horses obey; when they are not, they do not. The verse describes; it does not scold. It explains why good intentions so often fail.
analogy: Like a learner driver on an icy road with the wheel slipping through their hands: the engine is fine; what is missing is the hold.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That for one without understanding, whose mind is always unheld, the senses are out of control, like the vicious horses of a charioteer.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The charioteer called intellect, if unskilled and undiscerning in acting and refraining, «अनिपुणोऽविवेकी प्रवृत्तौ च निवृत्तौ च», with the mind, the reins, unheld and unsettled, «अप्रगृहीतेन असमाहितेन», finds the senses cannot be checked, «अशक्यनिवारणानि», like untamed horses, «अदान्ताश्वाः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He comments on 1.3.5–6 together: these two verses give the purpose of describing body and the rest as a chariot, «शरीरादेः रथत्वादिरूपणस्य प्रयोजनमाह». In the world horses are controlled when the charioteer and reins are sound; so the senses are controlled when understanding and mind are sound, and not otherwise, «नान्यथा इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

advaita.text: The verse describes the unskilled charioteer, the intellect, whose senses cannot be checked, «अशक्यनिवारणानि».

visistadvaita.text: The point of the chariot image: the senses are controlled only when understanding and mind are sound, «नान्यथा इत्यर्थः».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja read the verse alike as a description of control lost. In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

parallels.note: The Gītā: the mind that follows the roaming senses carries off understanding, as wind a boat.

parallels.quote: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्
parallels.note: Arjuna on the mind as restless, violent and strong — the same difficulty.

contemporary.text: The verse locates the trouble not in the horses but in the hold on the reins. That is a hopeful diagnosis: horses cannot be changed, but a grip can be learned. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: When did your senses last ‘bolt’ with you?
reflect.deeper: Why does the verse blame the lack of understanding rather than the senses?
reflect.practice: Choose one small habit of distraction and notice the moment just before it begins.

flags.note: madhva.json files Madhva’s single comment on 1.3.10–11 (his mark ॥ १०-१२ ॥) under every mantra from 1.3.3 to 1.3.11; it is not quoted here.
